notes.meaning: When the tribes receive their shares of the Promised Land, God tells them to set aside a special sacred section for Him first. This holy tract of ground belongs directly to the Lord before anyone else gets an allotment. It reminds the nation that God is the true owner of the land and must be at the center of their lives.

differ.view: Expect a literal division of the Promised Land among the tribes during a future earthly kingdom.
View this division symbolically as a picture of the spiritual growth, order, and beauty of the church under Christ.

notes.meaning: Inside this holy district, an area five hundred cubits square is reserved for the temple complex. An open border of fifty cubits surrounds the outer wall like a protective green space. This open ground keeps ordinary life from pressing directly against God's sacred house.

A large portion of the holy district is assigned to the priests who minister before the Lord. Their houses will be placed right around the Most Holy Place of the temple. Living near the sanctuary allows them to serve God faithfully and guard the sacred courts.

Another large area next to the priests' land belongs to the Levites, who assist in the daily work of the temple. In earlier times, Levite families were scattered across many towns, but here they receive a unified district. This land provides them with towns where they can live securely while caring for the temple.

A narrower strip running beside the holy district is set aside for the city. This area belongs to all twelve tribes together rather than to any single tribe. It provides room and food for the workers from every part of Israel who come to serve the city.

The prince receives large tracts of land on both the east and west sides of the sacred central district. His property stretches all the way to the Mediterranean Sea on one side and the Jordan River on the other. Giving the ruler an ample personal estate gives him enough wealth to support his government with dignity.

Because the prince has rich land of his own, he will have no excuse to seize fields from the people. Earlier rulers in Israel had often abused their power by stealing family lands, like King Ahab did with Naboth. God's leaders are commanded to protect their neighbors rather than exploit them.

The Lord commands Israel's rulers to put an immediate end to violence, looting, and heavy burdens. God tells them that their past cruelty is more than enough and demands that they govern with honest justice. Authority from God is meant to shield the weak instead of driving them out of their homes.

God demands complete honesty in everyday buying and selling through accurate scales and standard containers. The dry measure, called an ephah, and the liquid measure, called a bath, must both hold exactly one-tenth of a larger homer. Silver weights must also be dependable and true, showing that God cares about fairness in our daily work.

God explains the regular contribution the people must give from their crops and flocks to support worship. They are to set aside a sixtieth of their grain, a hundredth of their olive oil, and one sheep out of every two hundred. These gifts supply the sacrifices needed to make atonement, which means restoring peace and fellowship between a holy God and sinful people.

Every person in the country is required to share in bringing this regular contribution to the prince. No family is left out, showing that supporting God's worship is a joint duty for the whole community. The people give these gifts willingly so their leader can represent them in public worship.

The prince uses the people's contributions to provide all the regular sacrifices for weekly Sabbaths, monthly New Moons, and yearly feast days. He supplies the animals, grain, wine, and oil to atone for the entire nation. By leading the public worship, the ruler serves as a spiritual sponsor for all Israel.

differ.view: Understands this prince as a picture of Jesus Christ, who provides the ultimate sacrifice to atone for His people once for all.
Believes the prince is a human earthly leader in a future kingdom age, since he must offer sacrifices for his own sins and has natural children.

notes.meaning: On the first day of the new year, a young bull without defects is offered to purify the sanctuary. The priest places some of the sacrificial blood on the temple doorposts, the corners of the altar, and the inner court gate. This ceremony cleans away any ritual uncleanness so that God can dwell in holiness among His people.

One week later, on the seventh day of the month, the priest repeats this cleansing for the temple. This special offering covers sins committed by mistake or out of simple ignorance. God graciously provides a way to wipe away the spiritual harm caused even by faults people did not realize they had done.

On the fourteenth day of the first month, the people celebrate Passover and eat bread made without yeast for seven full days. This festival looked back to the night God rescued Israel from slavery in Egypt. In this vision, the feast also keeps the people focused on purity and thanksgiving before God.

On Passover day, the prince provides a bull as a sin offering for himself and for all the people. A sin offering is a sacrifice made to wipe away the guilt of wrongdoing. Offering for himself makes it clear that the prince is a regular human being who needs God's mercy just like everyone else.

Every day during the seven days of Passover, the prince supplies seven bulls and seven rams as burnt offerings, along with a male goat for a sin offering. He also provides generous baskets of flour and olive oil to go with each animal. The large number of animals shows an outpouring of dedication and wholehearted worship to the Lord.

Six months later, during the autumn Feast of Shelters, the prince provides the very same sacrifices for each of its seven days. This festival remembered how God sheltered Israel in tents in the desert and gave them good harvests. Repeating these full offerings reminds the nation that ongoing cleansing and thankful hearts are always needed before God.
